slides.heading: Design Facebook News Feed
slides.subtitle: SystemsExpert design walkthrough
slides.narration: In this lecture we design Facebook News Feed. We'll follow the interview framework: clarify, set requirements, estimate, sketch the architecture, define the data and API, then dive into the hard parts and the trade-offs.

slides.heading: Clarifying questions
bullets: Ranked or chronological?
Text only or media too?
Friends only, or pages/groups?
How fresh must the feed be?
slides.narration: Start by clarifying the scope with your interviewer. Good questions here are: Ranked or chronological? Text only or media too? Friends only, or pages or groups? How fresh must the feed be?

slides.heading: Functional requirements
bullets: Create posts
See a feed of friends' posts
Like/comment counts on posts
slides.narration: The functional requirements. Create posts. See a feed of friends' posts. Like or comment counts on posts.

slides.heading: Non-functional requirements
bullets: Feed load p95 < 500 ms
Eventual consistency acceptable (seconds)
Billions of users, highly available
slides.narration: The non-functional requirements. Feed load p95 under 500 ms. Eventual consistency acceptable (seconds). Billions of users, highly available.

slides.heading: Capacity estimates
bullets: ~2B users, ~1B DAU, each opens feed ~10x/day -> ~100k feed reads/s avg, ~300k peak
~500M posts/day -> ~6k writes/s
Average ~500 friends; celebrities millions of followers
slides.narration: Now some rough capacity estimates, which drive the design. about 2B users, about 1B DAU, each opens feed about 10x per day to about 100k feed reads per s avg, about 300k peak. about 500M posts per day to about 6k writes per s. Average about 500 friends; celebrities millions of followers.

slides.heading: Capacity: worked out
bullets: 1B DAU × 10 opens/day = 10B reads/day
500M posts/day ≈ 6k writes/s
Fan-out: 6k/s × 500 friends ≈ 3M cache writes/s
slides.narration: Let's actually work the numbers. A billion daily users each opening the feed ten times is ten billion reads a day. That's about a hundred fifteen thousand reads a second, and around three hundred fifty thousand at peak. Five hundred million posts a day is about six thousand writes a second. Fanning each out to five hundred friends means about three million cache writes a second, which is why celebrities are handled differently.

slides.heading: High-level architecture
slides.narration: Here's the high-level architecture. Client connects to API. API connects to Post service and Feed service. Post service connects to Posts DB sharded by post id and Post-created stream. Post-created stream connects to Fan-out workers. Fan-out workers connects to Feed cache: user to post ids. Feed service connects to Feed cache: user to post ids and Ranking service and Posts DB sharded by post id. Social graph connects to Fan-out workers.

slides.heading: Request flow: Open the feed
slides.caption: 1. User opens the app
slides.narration: Let's follow a feed load. The user opens the app and requests the first page of the feed.

slides.heading: Request flow: Open the feed
slides.caption: 2. API routes to feed service
slides.narration: The API authenticates and calls the feed service.

slides.heading: Request flow: Open the feed
slides.caption: 3. Read precomputed post IDs
slides.narration: The feed service reads the user's precomputed list of post IDs from the feed cache, built earlier by fan-out workers.

slides.heading: Request flow: Open the feed
slides.caption: 4. Cache returns candidates
slides.narration: The cache returns a few hundred candidate post IDs. Posts from celebrities are pulled at read time instead and merged in.

slides.heading: Request flow: Open the feed
slides.caption: 5. Rank candidates
slides.narration: The ranking service scores the candidates for this user, using engagement predictions and freshness.

slides.heading: Request flow: Open the feed
slides.caption: 6. Hydrate the top posts
slides.narration: Finally we hydrate the top posts with their content from the posts store and return the page.

slides.heading: Data model
bullets: posts(id, author_id, body, media_urls, created_at)
edges(user_id, friend_id)
feed_cache: user_id -> list of (post_id, score) capped ~500
slides.narration: Here is the data model. The posts record holds id, author id, body, media urls, created at. The edges record holds user id, friend id. feed cache: user id to list of (post id, score) capped about 500.

slides.heading: API
slides.narration: The API. The main endpoints are: POST posts; GET feed with cursor equals and limit equals 20. Each one is small, resource-oriented and easy to version.

slides.heading: Fan-out on write vs read
bullets: Push post ids into followers' precomputed feeds for normal users (fast reads).
For celebrities (> ~10k followers) skip fan-out and merge their recent posts at read time - hybrid model.
slides.narration: Deep dive: Fan-out on write versus read. Push post ids into followers' precomputed feeds for normal users (fast reads). For celebrities ( over about 10k followers) skip fan-out and merge their recent posts at read time - hybrid model.

slides.heading: Ranking
bullets: Feed service fetches candidate ids, hydrates posts in batch, scores with a model (affinity, recency, engagement) and paginates with a stable cursor.
slides.narration: Deep dive: Ranking. Feed service fetches candidate ids, hydrates posts in batch, scores with a model (affinity, recency, engagement) and paginates with a stable cursor.

slides.heading: Storage
bullets: Posts in a sharded KV/SQL store; media in blob store + CDN; feed cache in Redis/Memcache clusters sharded by user_id, rebuildable from source.
slides.narration: Deep dive: Storage. Posts in a sharded KV or SQL store; media in blob store plus CDN; feed cache in Redis or Memcache clusters sharded by user id, rebuildable from source.

slides.heading: Key decisions
bullets: Fan-out on write for most users → fast reads
Fan-out on read for celebrities → avoids millions of writes per post
Feed cache stores IDs only → small, cheap to update
Separate ranking service → iterate on models independently
slides.narration: Let's pull together the key decisions. Fan-out on write for most users, because fast reads. Fan-out on read for celebrities, because avoids millions of writes per post. Feed cache stores IDs only, because small, cheap to update. Separate ranking service, because iterate on models independently.

slides.heading: Trade-offs & alternatives
bullets: Precomputed feeds use a lot of memory but give low latency
Hybrid fan-out adds read-time merge complexity
Eventual consistency means your own post may appear slightly late - write-through to your own feed fixes it
slides.narration: Finally, the key trade-offs. Precomputed feeds use a lot of memory but give low latency. Hybrid fan-out adds read-time merge complexity. Eventual consistency means your own post may appear slightly late - write-through to your own feed fixes it.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Clarify scope, then functional + non-functional needs
Estimate load to size storage and fan-out
Core pieces: Client, API, Post service, Posts DB sharded by post_id, Post-created stream
Know your trade-offs and failure modes
slides.narration: To recap Facebook News Feed: we clarified the scope, set functional and non-functional requirements, estimated the load, sketched an architecture built around Client, API, Post service, Posts DB sharded by post id, and walked through the deep dives and trade-offs. Practise explaining each decision out loud.
